d.title: Six modalities, and the hard part is in none of these columns
d.caption: **The difficulty is not processing each one — module 5 showed a transformer handles images by tokenising patches** — it is **aligning representations so that a vector derived from pixels and a vector derived from words can be meaningfully compared.** Read the third column: every modality has a working tokenisation, **so the input problem is solved and the comparison problem is what §05 is about.**

d.title: LLaVA has no cross-attention module and gets cross-attention anyway
d.caption: **It projects patches into the LLM's embedding space so they become ordinary tokens — and because self-attention then runs over text and visual tokens together, the *effect* is cross-modal attention in every layer.** So it achieves cross-attention fusion without a cross-attention module, which is why the architecture diagram is so much simpler than Flamingo's. The fusion point is the real axis: **CLIP has zero interaction, the bridges interact everywhere, and the bottlenecks interact through a fixed number of slots.**

state: a fixed latent array, any input

d.title: Thirty-two vectors, whatever the resolution
d.caption: 5.9 computed the problem this solves: **a 1024-pixel image at patch 14 is 5,329 visual tokens, 130% of a 4k context.** BLIP-2's Q-Former uses **32 learned query vectors that cross-attend to the image features and output 32 tokens, regardless of resolution**; Flamingo's Perceiver Resampler does it with 64. **The image cost becomes a constant rather than a function of resolution, which is what makes multi-image and video input feasible at all.** The trade is explicit: **whatever those 32 vectors miss is gone — and small text in a document is exactly what a fixed-size summary loses.**

nodes.label: So image cost is a constant
And whatever they miss is gone

d.title: Three ways to align, and they differ by a factor of three hundred in what you train
d.caption: **Contrastive alignment trains both encoders and needs enormous paired data — 400M pairs for CLIP. Projection alignment freezes a good vision encoder and a good LLM and trains a small bridge: about 21M parameters against a 7B model.** Joint training updates everything on interleaved data and is what the largest native-multimodal models do. **So the question is not which is best but what you have: paired data, two good frozen models, or a training budget.**

d.title: Two encoders, no cross-attention, one shared space
d.caption: The architecture is deliberately minimal: **two towers that never interact, trained so that matching pairs have high cosine similarity and non-matching pairs low — on 400M (image, text) pairs.** 5.9 measured the real checkpoint: **87,456,000 vision parameters, 63,165,952 text parameters, a 512-dimensional shared space, and a learned temperature that saturated at exactly 100.00.** The absence of interaction is the feature: **both sides can be embedded offline and compared with a dot product, which is what makes retrieval at scale possible.**

d.title: 0.000284 for perfect alignment and 6.0767 for none, against a chance level of 2.0794
d.caption: The loss is symmetric cross-entropy over the similarity matrix, and the three numbers bracket it exactly. **Perfect alignment gives 0.000284; random data gives 6.0767 — which is nearly three times the chance level of `ln(8) = 2.0794`, not equal to it.** That is the temperature's doing: **at `T = 0.07` the softmax is sharp, so a wrong ranking is confidently wrong rather than merely unhelpful**, which §04 measures directly.

d.title: The batch is the negative set, so batch size is the difficulty of the task
d.caption: **Every other item in the batch is a negative, so a batch of 8 asks the model to pick the right caption out of 8 and a batch of 32,768 asks it to pick out of 32,768.** Which makes batch size a **capability** parameter rather than a throughput one: `ln(batch)` is the chance-level loss, and **it rises from 2.08 to 10.40 across this table.** That is why CLIP trained at 32,768 and why SigLIP's sigmoid loss — **which scores each pair independently — was a real architectural contribution rather than a tweak.**

d.title: At T=0.01 the loss on random data is 40.62
d.caption: **At `T = 1.00` the loss on random data is 2.1244 — essentially the chance level of 2.0794, because the softmax is flat enough that being wrong costs little. At `T = 0.01` it is 40.62, because a very sharp softmax converts a slightly wrong ranking into a near-certain wrong answer.** CLIP initialises at **0.07 and learns the value from there**, which is 5.9's `logit_scale` saturating at 100.00 — **so the model chose to be sharp, and the loss landscape at low temperature is why that choice has to be learned rather than set.**

d.title: Three of four right, with no training, and the failure is the interesting one
d.caption: Four programmatically generated images and four captions, **no training, no labels, no fine-tuning — and the three shapes are classified at 0.9950, 0.9998 and 1.0000.** The failure is the block of horizontal bars standing in for printed text: **CLIP calls it a square at 0.7000.** Which is a reasonable mistake — **a filled rectangular region of bars does look like a square to a patch-based encoder** — and a useful reminder that these confidences are **not calibrated**: 0.70 on a wrong answer and 1.00 on a right one are both produced by the same sharp temperature.

d.title: The same image, 0.9951 down to 0.7440, on phrasing alone
d.caption: **Four phrasings of the same concept against the same image: `“a photo of a red circle”` 0.9951, `“a red circle”` 0.9874, `“red circle”` 0.9811, `“circle”` 0.7440.** So the prompt template is worth a quarter of the score here, **which is why `“a photo of a {}”` is the standard CLIP template and why published zero-shot numbers use prompt ensembles.** The mechanism is simple: **CLIP was trained on captions, and a bare noun is not a caption** — so the text tower sees it as out of distribution.

d.title: Five variants, and each one names a specific defect of the original
d.caption: Read the right-hand column as a list of CLIP's problems. **OpenCLIP exists because the original training data was never released — a reproducibility failure, not a technical one. SigLIP's sigmoid loss removes the giant-batch requirement §03 measured.** EVA-CLIP attacks fine detail with a better ViT and higher resolution. **And MetaCLIP and ALIGN are the two sides of one argument: curated metadata against 1.8B noisy pairs — data quality against raw scale.**

d.title: Three patterns, and the middle one is the whole open-source ecosystem
d.caption: **Dual encoders do similarity only, so they retrieve and classify and cannot answer a question. The bridge pattern — vision encoder, connector, LLM — is what every open VLM is**, and the variation between them is the connector: **LLaVA uses an MLP, BLIP-2 uses 32 learned queries, Flamingo uses gated cross-attention.** Native multimodal trains all modalities in one stack from pretraining, **which is the only pattern that generates as well as understands.**

d.title: The LLM will process anything you hand it, sensibly or not
d.caption: **Its layers were trained on inputs with a particular scale and geometry — a specific typical norm, a specific distribution across dimensions — and nothing checks that what arrives resembles that.** So the projector's job is not only dimensional (**1024 → 4096**) but **distributional**: produce vectors that sit where token embeddings sit. The scale reference makes it concrete — **GPT-2's token embeddings have std 0.1437 and mean norm 3.9585** — and **a projector whose output norm is ten times that will be attended to as if it were a shouting token.**

nodes.label: So the projector is learned, not derived
nodes.sub: it has to find that geometry

d.title: A few hundred thousand caption pairs would overwrite the language ability
d.caption: **Training the LLM directly on image-caption pairs is catastrophic forgetting: a narrow fine-tuning distribution overwriting broad pretrained capability.** So stage 1 **teaches the projector to speak the LLM's language without touching the LLM at all**, and stage 2 unfreezes it on instruction data once the visual tokens already land in the right place. Which is the same reasoning as Flamingo's zero-initialised gate in 5.9 — **both designs start from exactly the original model and add visual influence from there.**

nodes.label: Train the LLM on caption pairs
Same logic as Flamingo's zero gate

d.title: Fluent, confident and wrong — and one prefix fixes it
d.caption: BLIP at 224M parameters on three synthetic images: **a red circle becomes `'a white circle with a black dot on it'`, and two blue squares become `"a blue square icon with the word ' s logo"`.** Fluent English, confidently wrong, **and nothing in the output signals the failure.** Then the conditional runs: **the prefix `'there are'` produces `'there are two squares'` — correct — while `'a picture of'` produces a degenerate loop of apostrophes.** So **the prompt is doing more work than the image here**, which is the honest reading of small-VLM captioning.

state: 'a white circle with a black dot'
"a blue square icon with the word"

d.title: Forty-eight times smaller, at every resolution
d.caption: **Stable Diffusion's VAE downsamples 8× spatially into 4 channels, and the compression is exactly 48.0× at every resolution** — which is the point of latent diffusion: **the expensive iterative process runs on 16,384 numbers instead of 786,432.** And because the ratio is constant, **resolution scales the cost of the denoiser linearly in pixels rather than changing the method** — so a 1024×1024 image is a 65,536-element latent, still well inside what a U-Net or DiT handles.

d.title: Correlation with the original crosses zero at step 700
d.caption: **`alpha_bar` falls from 0.9999 to 0.000040 over 1000 steps, and the correlation between `z_t` and `z_0` goes 0.9999 → 0.5307 at step 300 → −0.0017 at step 700.** So **by step 700 the noised latent carries no linear information about the original at all** — which is what “pure noise” means operationally, and why the schedule's tail is relatively uninformative. Note the signal coefficient at step 500 is **0.2789**: a quarter of the original is still present where the correlation is already down to 0.1755.

d.title: Predicting noise and predicting the image are algebraically the same choice
d.caption: **Given `ε`, recovering the clean latent is one line of algebra — and with the true `ε` the max absolute error is 4.06e-07**, which is float noise. So the network could equally be trained to predict `z_0` directly: **the two parameterisations are related by an exact invertible formula.** The reason `ε` wins is practical rather than mathematical — **its target has roughly unit variance at every timestep, while `z_0`'s does not, so the loss is comparably scaled across the whole schedule.**

state: predicting eps or z_0 is one choice

d.title: Guidance extrapolates past the conditional prediction, and doubles the cost
d.caption: **At `w = 1.0` the result *is* the conditional prediction — distance 0.0000. Above that, guidance extrapolates: at `w = 7.5` the output is 1.5244 away from the conditional and nowhere near either input.** Which is why high guidance produces saturated, over-committed images: **it is an extrapolation, not an interpolation.** And the cost is structural: **every step needs both a conditional and an unconditional forward pass, so 50 steps is 100 U-Net calls** — a permanent doubling, and why distilled-guidance models are an active area.

d.title: Five control mechanisms, and two of them need no training at all
d.caption: **Inpainting and Img2Img are sampling tricks: re-impose the unmasked latent at every step so only the masked area changes, or start from a partially noised real image so the noise level sets how much survives.** Neither trains anything. **ControlNet's zero-initialised convolutions are the same idea as Flamingo's gate — at the start of training the condition has no effect, so the base model is preserved exactly.** And the last row changes the subject rather than the style: **teaching the model a *specific* subject from a handful of images.**

items.label: Inpainting
items.sub: re-impose the unmasked latent each step

items.label: Img2Img
items.sub: start from a partially noised real image

items.label: DreamBooth / Textual Inversion
items.sub: one specific subject from a few images

d.title: The U-Net is becoming a transformer and CLIP is becoming T5
d.caption: Two trends are visible in four rows. **The U-Net is being replaced by a transformer (DiT) in SD3 and Flux — which is 5.7's convergence again: once you can tokenise the input, the transformer block works.** And **the text encoder is moving from CLIP to T5**, in Imagen 3 and DALL-E 3's better captioner, **which addresses the conditioning weakness directly: CLIP's text tower was trained for retrieval, not for carrying compositional detail into a generator.**

d.title: Thirty seconds of audio would be 2.3e+11 attention entries
d.caption: **16 kHz means 480,000 samples for thirty seconds, and as tokens that is 2.30e+11 attention entries per head per layer.** Which is **identical to the image problem in 5.7: the natural representation has far more elements than a quadratic-cost mechanism can accept** — and the solution is identical too. **Do not tokenise the raw signal. For images that meant patches; for audio it means a spectrogram.**

d.title: A 10 ms hop gives 5 to 15 frames per phoneme, which is the whole reason for the number
d.caption: **Phonemes last roughly 50–150 ms, so a 10 ms frame gives 5 to 15 frames per phoneme — enough to see the transitions that distinguish one from another. At 100 ms hops a whole phoneme might occupy a single frame and the distinguishing detail is gone.** So **the hop size is a resolution choice made against the physics of speech, not an arbitrary hyperparameter.** And the arithmetic lands somewhere convenient: **3000 frames halved by a stride-2 convolution, so Whisper's encoder always sees exactly 1500 tokens.**

d.title: The decoder is 78% of Whisper, which is the reverse of a vision model
d.caption: **8,208,384 parameters in the encoder and 29,552,256 in the decoder — 22% against 78%.** The reason is in the last row: **the decoder has a 51,865-entry multilingual vocabulary with language tags, and 5.7 showed an embedding table is where a vocabulary's cost lands.** So Whisper is mostly a language model that happens to be conditioned on audio, **which is also why it hallucinates fluent text on silence: the decoder is strong enough to continue plausibly without the encoder.**

d.title: A sixty-second clip at 24 fps is 1.36e+11 attention entries
d.caption: **At 256 tokens per frame, one second at 8 fps is 2,048 tokens and sixty seconds at 24 fps is 368,640** — which is 1.36e+11 attention entries, the same order as thirty seconds of raw audio in §01. So **video is not a harder version of the image problem, it is the image problem multiplied by frame rate**, and every strategy in the table is a way of not paying it. Note what each costs: **sparse sampling misses fast motion, pooling loses spatial detail in every frame, and a bottleneck loses whatever its queries miss.**

d.title: Fourteen point eight times cheaper, and one thing becomes impossible
d.caption: **16 frames × 196 patches is 3,136 tokens: joint attention is 9,834,496 entries, and a spatial pass followed by a temporal pass is 664,832 — 14.8× cheaper.** The saving is real and so is the loss, and it is specific: **no single-hop cross-frame, cross-patch attention.** A patch in frame 1 can reach a patch in frame 16 **only via a shared position** — so a moving object that changes location between frames needs two hops, **which is exactly the dependency video is about.**

d.title: Five models, and only one of them is an encoder-decoder
d.caption: **Whisper is the only encoder-decoder here, and the only one doing recognition rather than generation** — everything else is autoregressive over audio tokens. Which is the structural split worth noticing: **recognition maps a long signal to a short sequence, so an encoder-decoder fits; generation maps a short prompt to a long signal, so a decoder does.** And **VALL-E's three-second enrollment is the number that makes voice cloning a safety question rather than a research one.**

d.title: One space, and the queries can cross
d.caption: The mechanism is just §02's shared space with more encoders attached — **and what it buys is that a query in one modality retrieves in another: text finds images, an image finds descriptions, audio finds video clips.** The models differ only in how many towers they bind: **CLIP two, CLAP two, ImageBind six — image, text, audio, depth, thermal and IMU.** Which raises the question §04 answers: **you cannot have paired data for all fifteen modality pairs, so how is six achieved?**

nodes.label: So a query can cross modalities
CLIP 2, CLAP 2, ImageBind 6
nodes.sub: the only difference is the count

d.title: Three of three, on a margin of 0.03 to 0.10
d.caption: **Every query retrieves the right image — and the diagonal values are 0.2857, 0.3191 and 0.3493 against off-diagonals in the 0.21–0.25 range.** So the retrieval works on **a margin of about 0.03 to 0.10, with every absolute value in a narrow band**, which is 3.6's anisotropy appearing a third time. **Read the gap, not the score: 0.2857 sounds like weak evidence and it is the strongest cell in its row.**

d.title: Text-to-text similarity works, on a pairing the loss never compared
d.caption: **CLIP's contrastive loss only ever compares images against texts — it never scores two texts against each other. And yet: `'a red circle'` against `'a crimson round shape'` is 0.8064, while against `'a blue square'` it is 0.6762.** Which is the property that makes a shared space more than a lookup table: **aligning both towers to each other forces structure *within* each tower**, so relationships the training objective never mentioned are nonetheless preserved. The dog/puppy pair at **0.9594 against 0.8323** shows it again.

d.title: Bind everything to images and six modalities share one space from five pair types
d.caption: **The observation is that images appear in all the natural pairings — captions give image-text, video with sound gives image-audio, RGBD cameras give image-depth, thermal cameras give image-thermal, video with motion sensors gives image-IMU.** So **you never need an audio-thermal dataset: bind each modality to images and all six end up in one space**, with the cross-pairs emerging the way §03's text-to-text similarity did. **Five pair types instead of fifteen**, and images are the only modality that could have served as the anchor.

d.title: Skip the parsing entirely: render the page and embed the image
d.caption: **PDF text extraction destroys exactly what makes documents comprehensible — table structure becomes a jumble of cells, figures vanish, column layout interleaves, and a chart's meaning disappears entirely.** ColPali's answer is to not do it: **render the page as an image and embed it with a vision model, so the document is preserved as the thing it actually is.** Which is 7.7's “position is semantics” argument taken to its conclusion — **if the layout carries the meaning, do not project it to one dimension at all.**

nodes.label: ColPali: render the page as an image

d.title: 1,240.00 means “total” because of where it sits
d.caption: **In an invoice, `1,240.00` means *total* because it sits in the bottom-right, aligned under a column headed *Amount*, on the row labelled *Total*. Strip the layout and you have a number with no role.** The same failure in two other forms: **a two-column paper extracted naively interleaves the columns into sentences that alternate between unrelated paragraphs, and a table flattened to a sequence leaves no cell knowing its row or column.** **The information was never in the characters — it was in the arrangement, and every text-extraction step is a lossy projection of a 2-D object onto a 1-D one.**

nodes.label: Bottom-right, under 'Amount', row 'Total'
nodes.sub: THAT is what makes it the total

nodes.label: A table -> cells with no row or column

d.title: Six models, and two of them delete a pipeline stage
d.caption: **Donut is OCR-free — image straight to structured output, with no OCR stage at all — and Nougat goes page image to LaTeX, preserving equations.** Both remove the step that §06 identifies as the biggest error source. The others keep the stages and improve one each: **LayoutLM adds 2-D position to the transformer, TrOCR replaces the OCR model, Table Transformer treats rows and columns as objects to detect.** Which is the real choice in document AI: **fix a stage, or remove it.**

d.title: Four extra numbers per token, and that is the whole idea
d.caption: **A text transformer embeds a token and adds a 1-D positional encoding for its index in the sequence. LayoutLM adds 2-D positional embeddings as well — the token's bounding box — so the model knows not just that a word is fifth but that it sits at a particular x and y.** Plus image patch features for the visual appearance. **Which is small and effective, and it is 4.9's positional-encoding question asked in two dimensions**: the same mechanism, with the grid that ViT's flattened 1-D table threw away.
vars: what is added to the token embedding

d.title: Five error sources, and the most damaging one is the least noticed
d.caption: **Layout misdetection is first for a reason: a merged table region or a missed column boundary corrupts everything downstream, and OCR will happily read the wrong crop** — producing confident text from the wrong part of the page. Reading order is the subtle one: **text that is individually correct, assembled into nonsense.** And the last row is the trap: **sending the page to a general VLM feels like it skips all of this, and 7.3 measured what that costs — fluent, confident, wrong.**

items.label: Layout misdetection
items.sub: most damaging, least noticed - OCR reads the wrong crop

items.label: Table structure
items.sub: detecting a table exists is far easier than its grid

d.title: Three metrics, and two of them score a distribution rather than an image
d.caption: **FID and IS both measure quality *and* diversity together, over a set — so neither can score a single image, and a model that produces one perfect picture every time scores badly on both.** FID is a Fréchet distance between real and generated feature distributions in Inception-v3 space, which means **it inherits whatever Inception-v3 is sensitive to.** LPIPS is the odd one out: **a learned perceptual distance between two specific images, so it needs a reference and answers a different question.**

d.title: One of these needs no reference caption, which is why it gets used
d.caption: **CLIPScore's appeal is that it is reference-free — you need only the image and the candidate, not human captions to compare against — which makes it usable at scale where CIDEr and SPICE are not.** The others all need references: **CIDEr wants several, SPICE parses both into scene graphs, and BLEU/ROUGE/METEOR are 3.4's text metrics with all their limits.** The question §03 answers is whether reference-free also means useful.

d.title: The wrong count scores higher than the right one
d.caption: The image has **exactly two blue squares**, and the measurement is damning: **`'one blue square'` scores 0.6741 against the correct `'two blue squares'` at 0.6717 — the wrong caption wins by +0.0023.** Meanwhile wrong colour costs −0.0595 and wrong shape −0.0482, **so CLIPScore sees colour and shape and is blind to number.** And the longest caption scores highest at **0.7028**: **length and specificity inflate it somewhat independently of accuracy**, which matters before comparing captioners with different output lengths.

d.title: A metric that admits the ground truth is a distribution
d.caption: **Ten annotators answer each question. Three or more giving your answer scores 1.0; one gives 0.33.** The definition exists because **visual questions frequently have several defensible answers — *what colour is the shirt?* on a shirt that is arguably blue or arguably teal — and a binary exact-match metric would call a reasonable answer wrong.** Which is **a more honest framing than most benchmarks use**, and it has a price: **ten human annotations per question, so it exists only for the datasets that paid for it.**

nodes.label: So the truth is a distribution
